# Model Principles {.unnumbered}

The repair task begins with a model call that proposes an inspection or a patch. The call consumes resources even when its output is unusable, and a complete response still leaves the runtime to check what it proposes. Part I makes this boundary concrete. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model establishes what a request supplies, how the response reports completion, and how input and output contribute to cost. @Sec-vol3-test-time-compute then considers how longer generation, additional candidates, and feedback change the chance of obtaining a useful result within a fixed budget. Neither a more expensive call nor a larger collection of proposals grants authority to act. A single call has no horizon beyond itself, carries no state forward, and holds no authority, so the single call is the origin from which the later parts measure each departure. Test-time compute takes the first step away from that origin. Every extra model call or check spent inside one decision adds a turn to the horizon, which is why that spending needs a ceiling before the agent acts on anything. In the agent stack of @sec-vol3-intro-stochastic-computer, Part I studies the processor.

A request can include a long source excerpt and ask for a short edit, or ask the model to reproduce the entire changed file. Those choices impose different amounts of input processing and output generation. Autoregressive output conditions each token on the preceding sequence; in the ordinary token-by-token implementation, each additional token adds another generation step. The time per step depends on the serving configuration, so the engineering rule concerns a measured cost rather than a universal ratio.

::: {#pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding .callout-principle title="Output-bound latency"}

**Invariant**: Under a fixed serving configuration with approximately stable generation time per token, output-generation latency grows approximately with output length. For unbatched decoding of a dense model with $\Parameters$ parameters stored at $\ElementStorageSize$ bytes each, where weight reads dominate, memory bandwidth $\Bandwidth$ bounds each output token's step time from below:
$$ \PertokenDecodeTime \ge \frac{\Parameters\,\ElementStorageSize}{\Bandwidth} $$
The bound describes neither every serving configuration nor the whole call's latency, which also includes preparation, queueing, prefill, and postprocessing.

**Implication**: When generation dominates the call, an interface that expresses the same useful proposal in fewer tokens can reduce latency. Input processing, queueing, and checks must still fit the task's deadline. Compare interfaces at a matched task budget rather than assuming that shorter output is always better. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost develops the bound (@eq-vol3-fm-token-floors) and prices a concrete call; @sec-vol3-appendix-inference-roofline derives the hardware estimate and its assumptions.

:::

The runtime must also distinguish time spent from work completed. A call interrupted by a limit, a cancellation, or a lost connection may leave a partial payload, even if that payload parses. Completion status therefore precedes handling the output as a finished candidate, a mechanical gate that invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}) places below the model. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract develops this gate without treating a completed generation as evidence that the task succeeded. Additional inference then raises two separate questions: whether a useful candidate is available and whether the system can identify it. For the repair, generating several patches may expose alternatives that one call missed. A compiler can reject some of them, and a regression test can distinguish others. Neither check establishes every property of the intended repair, and selection can exploit a weak check as well as a useful one, making the scope of the check part of the design.

::: {#pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry .callout-principle title="The verification asymmetry"}

**Invariant**: Producing a valid candidate, selecting it, and establishing that it satisfies the task are different events. Additional sampling can raise the chance that a candidate set contains a valid result; the check that selects from the set bounds how far a pass can be trusted. For a valid-candidate rate $\ValidCandidateRate$, a false-reject rate $\VerifierFalseacceptanceFr$, and a false-accept rate $\VerifierFalseacceptance$, the precision of a passing verdict is
$$ \Pi_V = \frac{\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseacceptanceFr)}{\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseacceptanceFr)+(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\,\VerifierFalseacceptance} $$
A checker can be exact for a stated property and still leave open whether that property captures the task.

**Implication**: At a low valid rate, a small false-accept rate fills the passing set with invalid candidates, and the effect grows when a check becomes an optimization target, whether a selection rule over many samples or a training reward. Allocate a task's budget across generation, assessment, and feedback; compare the complete policy against a single-candidate baseline at matched cost, counting unsuccessful attempts and checks; and stop when marginal acceptance per unit cost falls below a threshold. State what each check supports, protect its criteria and observations from the actions it judges, and preserve unresolved requirements in the acceptance decision. Learned assessments can rank or revise candidates but supply neither permission to act nor an independent guarantee. @Sec-vol3-test-time-compute develops the precision (@eq-vol3-verifier-precision) and the stopping rule (@eq-vol3-marginal-stopping).

:::

These principles connect the price of a call to the responsibility for its result. The runtime bounds generation and handles incomplete responses, while candidate selection uses evidence whose limits remain explicit. The invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}) continues to govern both responsibilities. Part I supplies a usable model-call contract and a way to assess additional inference; the later parts supply the state, tools, and execution control needed to carry those decisions through a trajectory.
